prize_parts.citation: For establishing liquid-liquid phase separation and multivalent interactions as a physical-chemical principle by which biomolecules organize into membraneless compartments

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part on biomolecular phase separation, credited to Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen. The round-1 exchange sharpened what I am actually asking the committee to credit. It is the physical-chemical framework, not the claim that every cellular body is a liquid: Hyman and Brangwynne showed that P granules wet, fuse and drip like liquids (2009), and Rosen showed with defined multivalent proteins that the transition to a condensed phase follows from valency and affinity, with a measurable phase diagram. That core is quantitative, reproducible in vitro and in cells with controlled perturbations, and has been taken up across nucleolar, signalling, stress-granule and neurodegeneration research and in synthetic condensates. The citation I now propose is worded so that it stands even if the list of truly phase-separated assemblies in vivo keeps changing. It names a principle of molecular organisation, thermodynamics and phase behaviour applied to living matter, which is a different kind of contribution from a tool and gives the prize a physical-chemistry anchor.
statement.case_against: Two objections remain real. First, in-cell evidence is mixed: Brzezinski, Chabes, Linke and Zou are right that it is still contested which assemblies are phase separated at endogenous concentrations and what function that has, and a citation can only reduce this exposure, not remove it. Second, the three-name limit forces me to omit Pappu and Mittag, whose sequence-grammar and experimental work is substantial; I cannot defend that omission on scientific grounds, only on the argument that the founding demonstration and the multivalency framework are the most separable core. I also have to admit that no member other than me has this in a configuration, so a vote for it would currently be a minority position and I should say so plainly.

responses.point: Heiner treats B007 as a strong alternative, sides with Chabes and Brzezinski on maturity, and asks what is established beyond P-granule droplet behaviour; he himself proposes base editing (Liu) paired with sequencing by synthesis.
responses.response: His question is the right test, and I think it can be answered. Beyond P-granule behaviour, there is Rosen's reconstitution with defined multivalent proteins, where the onset of a condensed phase scales with valency and affinity as polymer theory predicts, and the nucleolus work that applied the same liquid criteria to a second compartment. Those are measurements of a phase diagram, which is the quantitative record he asks for. I accept that the in-cell functional meaning is open, which is why my citation is limited to the principle. On his own pairing, I find base editing more convincing as chemistry than I did in round 1, but I do not see how a read and a write technology form one achievement, and I would not trade a general concept for that coherence argument.

responses.point: Peter says the interpretive instability of phase separation makes it a candidate for a later year and the better alternative now if base editing fails on priority; he puts three names on base editing (Liu, Komor, Gaudelli).
responses.response: I take his point that instability argues for waiting, but I read the evidence differently. What is unstable is the catalogue of which cellular assemblies qualify, not the physical principle, and a prize for a principle is the situation in which it is safe to cite the framework and say nothing about the catalogue. On base editing, I notice that his three-name configuration is the one most exposed to the Kondo and Nishida question, because it uses all three slots and cannot also make room for them. If the committee goes that way, I would want the primary-paper dates before the trainees are credited, and I cannot judge them from what I was given.

responses.point: Xiaodong asks whether in-cell assemblies are established as phase-separated liquids, contrasts this with perovskites having a defined structure and independently confirmed performance, and doubts the chemistry framing is stronger than the cell-biology one.
responses.response: The structural question is fair and I agree the evidence for specific cellular assemblies is uneven. But the evidence that matters for my citation is the physical chemistry: phase boundaries, concentration thresholds and viscoelastic behaviour measured in defined systems, which are as quantitative as device efficiencies. On framing, I would say the chemistry is that multivalency and weak interactions set a thermodynamic phase boundary, which is the same reasoning I apply to lipids and surfactants; the cell biology is the application. I also share her concern about perovskite stability and lead toxicity, which is a reason I do not move toward B024.

responses.point: Andrei argues for base editing as a deamination reaction under programmable control, with a quantitative record, in the three-person Liu, Komor and Gaudelli configuration, and names sequencing as the safer alternative if base editing is judged too young.
responses.response: His argument that the adenine editor needed a deaminase evolved to act on DNA persuades me that base editing is more than a CRISPR accessory, and I am moving my view on that: I now regard it as a legitimate chemistry candidate and I keep it as my first alternative. I am not moving it to first place, because I still weigh breadth of concept above the strength of the engineering, and because the choice between Liu alone and a trainee structure is unresolved. He is right that the maturity of sequencing makes it a candidate that can wait, which is the reverse of the clinical-validation timing he assigns to base editing; I do not think either argument decides between the two of them.

responses.point: Johan moved in round 2 discussion from a single base-editing prize to a two-part prize with sequencing by synthesis, calling the attribution unusually clean (Liu; Balasubramanian and Klenerman).
responses.response: I follow his reasoning that clean attribution and a simple chemical idea are what a committee can defend, and the reversible terminator is a clean idea. My concern is that with three people in total, his pairing spends the whole budget on two DNA technologies, so the prize would say nothing about the physical chemistry of biomolecular organisation, which is a question Johan himself raises when he notes that his configuration leaves out the theory and physical-chemistry candidates. I would not call that a decisive objection, but it is the reason I stay with B007 rather than join this pairing.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a citation for the physical-chemical principle that is explicitly silent on which cellular assemblies are phase separated in vivo.
Whether omitting Pappu and Mittag is defensible; I cannot show that Rosen's slot should outrank either of them on scientific grounds alone.
Whether Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen can be framed as one achievement, with the P-granule demonstration and the multivalency framework as its two halves.

For base editing, which I now hold as my first alternative, the dates of Target-AID by Kondo and Nishida relative to the cytosine base editor, and whether credit should go to Liu alone, are not something I can settle from the files I was given.
That I am the only member with B007 in a configuration, which may mean I am underweighting the in-cell evidence problem that four colleagues have independently raised.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict changes since round 1 and none requires recusal. I am a Lund colleague of Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and my own work on lipid and amyloid assembly is adjacent to the physical chemistry of condensates, but I have no personal, institutional or funding tie to Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu, Mittag or any other named candidate. As the one member whose preferred part lies in my own broad field, I have tried to state its in-cell weaknesses at least as strongly as its strengths.
